articles.title: How to make a zine

body.support:
A **zine** (say *zeen*) is a small, home-made magazine. People make them about anything: food, sport, music, their town.

**1. Plan**

- **Topic:** what do you know about?
- **Audience:** who is it for?
- **Purpose:** to tell them something, make them laugh, or change their mind?
- Plan all **eight pages**.

**2. Write**

Write in your own words. Keep it short. Use headings and pictures.

**3. Your own work**

**Plagiarism** is copying someone's work and saying it's yours. Don't copy websites. Instead:

- use your own words and pictures
- put quotes in quote marks, and say who said it
- list your sources on the back.

**4. Fix it**

Read it out loud. Check capitals, full stops and spelling.

**5. Make it**

Fold one sheet into eight pages. Fill them. Copy it. Hand it out.
body.core:
A **zine** (say *zeen*) is a small, home-made magazine. People make them about anything: music, food, sport, their town, their job, a cause, a hobby. Most are photocopied and handed out, swapped or sold for a few dollars.

**Why make one?** Zines are cheap, quick and yours. No one edits them but you. And they're a great way to share something you know with people who need it.

**1. Plan**

- **Topic:** something you know or care about. *Cheap eats near TAFE. How to change a bike tyre. Best free things to do in our town.*
- **Audience:** who's it for? Year 11s? New apprentices? Your footy club?
- **Purpose:** to inform, entertain, or persuade?
- **Pages:** plan all eight. Cover, intro, a few info pages, tips, and a back page.

**2. Draft**

Write your pages in your own words. Keep it short: a zine page is small. Use **headings**, lists and pictures. Your first draft can be messy.

**3. Use your own work, or credit it**

**Plagiarism** is passing off someone else's work as your own. Copying a paragraph from a website, tracing a cartoon and signing it, or pasting in AI-written text without saying so are all plagiarism. Instead:

- use your own words, photos and drawings
- put a short **quote** in quote marks, and say who said it
- list your sources on the back page.

**4. Edit**

Read it out loud. Cut extra words. Check **capitals**, **full stops**, **spelling** and **paragraphs**. Ask someone from your audience to read it. Do they get it?

**5. Make it**

Fold one A4 sheet into eight pages, fill them, then photocopy. Hand copies out where your audience will find them.
body.extend:
A **zine** (pronounced *zeen*) is a small, self-published magazine, usually photocopied and distributed by hand. Zines cover every subject imaginable, from music and food to local history, activism, work and personal stories.

**Why zines?** They're inexpensive, quick to produce and entirely under the creator's control. That makes them an ideal way to share specialist knowledge with a specific audience.

**1. Plan.** Define your **topic**, **audience** and **purpose** (to inform, entertain or persuade). Map all eight pages: cover, introduction, content pages, practical tips and a back page with sources.

**2. Draft.** Write in your own voice. Space is tight, so use **headings**, lists and images, and prioritise what your audience most needs.

**3. Avoid plagiarism.** **Plagiarism** means presenting someone else's work (text, images or AI-generated content) as your own. Use original words and images. Quote briefly, in quotation marks, with attribution. **Credit** every source on your back page.

**4. Edit.** Revise for clarity and concision, then proofread for capitals, punctuation, spelling and paragraphing. Test it on a member of your audience.

**5. Produce and distribute.** Fold an A4 sheet into eight pages, complete the **layout**, photocopy it, and get copies to where your audience will find them.

caseStudies.title: Sticky Institute

body.support:
In **2001**, a small shop opened in Melbourne. It was in an underground walkway near Flinders Street Station. It was called **Sticky Institute**. It sold **zines**.

Anyone could make a zine and bring it in. People could use the photocopiers to make their own.

In **2008**, Sticky started a zine fair called the **Festival of the Photocopier**. The first one had about **50 tables**. By **2017**, it had **240 tables** at Melbourne Town Hall.

You don't need a publisher or lots of money. You need paper, a pen, a photocopier, and something to say.
body.core:
In **2001**, a small shop opened in the **Degraves Street subway**, the underground walkway near Flinders Street Station in Melbourne. It was called **Sticky Institute**, and it sold mostly one thing: **zines**.

Sticky was **artist-run**. Anyone could make a zine and bring it in. People could also use the shop's photocopiers and supplies to make their own.

In **2008**, Sticky started the **Festival of the Photocopier**, a fair where zine makers set up tables and sell or swap their work. The first one had about **50 tables** in the subway outside the shop. By **2017**, it had **240 tables** in the biggest rooms of Melbourne Town Hall.

The shop has moved since then. But the idea is the same: you don't need a publisher, a big budget or permission to share what you know. You need paper, a pen, a photocopier and something to say.

Zine makers write about anything: their suburb, their job, their favourite band, their mental health, their culture. Many make zines because nobody else is telling their story, or telling it the way they would.
body.extend:
In **2001**, **Sticky Institute** opened in the **Degraves Street subway**, the underground arcade near Melbourne's Flinders Street Station. It was an **artist-run** shop dedicated almost entirely to **zines**.

Sticky stocked zines from anyone who brought them in, and offered photocopiers and materials so people could produce their own.

In **2008**, it launched the **Festival of the Photocopier**, a zine fair where makers sell and swap their work. The first festival had about **50 tables** in the subway outside the shop. By **2017**, it had grown to **240 tables** in the largest rooms of Melbourne Town Hall.

The shop has since moved, but its premise remains: publishing doesn't require a publisher, a budget or permission. It requires paper, a photocopier and something worth saying.

Zine makers cover their suburbs, workplaces, music, health, identity and culture, often because mainstream media isn't telling their stories, or isn't telling them their way.

pages.instructions: Make your zine from one sheet of A4 paper, then copy it and hand it out to your audience.

support: Fold the paper into eight boxes.
Cut along the middle crease, halfway.
Fold it into a little book.
Fill each page from your plan.
Copy it and hand it out.
core: **Fold:** fold the A4 sheet in half, then in half again, then once more. Unfold. You'll see eight boxes.
**Cut:** fold it in half the short way. Cut along the middle crease from the folded edge, stopping halfway.
**Fold into a book:** open it, fold it the long way, then push the ends together so the cut opens into a diamond. Flatten it into an eight-page booklet.
**Fill:** add your words, headings and pictures to each page, following your plan. Keep text away from the edges.
**Copy and hand out:** unfold it flat, photocopy it, fold the copies, and give them to your audience. Ask one reader what they thought.

teacher.overview: The Everyday Texts boss level. Students plan, draft, edit and produce an eight-page zine (a one-sheet folded booklet) on a topic they know, for a real audience and purpose, using original words and images and crediting anything borrowed. They annotate a model zine, sort examples of plagiarism, plan all eight pages, draft and peer-edit two pages, then fold, fill, copy and distribute their zine. The case study is Melbourne's Sticky Institute, an artist-run zine shop opened in 2001 in the Degraves Street subway, which started the Festival of the Photocopier zine fair in 2008.
prep: A4 paper, scissors, black fine-liners, glue; access to a photocopier.
Practise the eight-page fold yourself, and make a demo zine.
Optional: bring in a few real zines (local libraries often have collections).
Check your school's policy on AI use, and make expectations clear.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** a small, home-made magazine, usually photocopied (e.g. cheap eats, a sport, your town). Passing off someone else's work as your own; use your own words and pictures, quote with credit, list sources. Clarity, extra words, capitals, full stops, spelling, paragraphs.

**Zine:** 1 cover; 2 intro; 3 info pages with headings and own photos; 4 tips; 5 credited quote with permission; 6 back page with maker, date and sources.

**Sort:** copied blog paragraph — plagiarism; own photos — OK; credited quote — OK; traced cartoon — plagiarism; uncredited AI page — plagiarism; own words with source listed — OK.

**Case study:** zines are cheap, physical, personal and local; the festival grew because people wanted to make and share their own work; answers will vary.

realityCheck: **The fold confuses people.** Demo it live, slowly, twice.
**Black pen copies best.** Pencil and light colours disappear on the photocopier.
**Topic choice is everything.** Push students towards something they genuinely know.
**Distribution makes it real.** Even leaving copies in the library or canteen counts.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Cheap, hands-on, and students are proud of the result.
